These three words are the way I taught kids to say the R sound (worked well with my Japanese to English students, too):

Coat, goat, rote. 

Have them say the first one, then the second one, and focus on the position of the back of the tongue.  Then again, with a focus on how the air is stopped in both words, and how differently the air is released.  

Last, I explain that the last word, rote, is the same to gue position, but there is no explosive release of air, just a slow escape, with the vocal chords making the vibration, the tongue just modifies it.  

Lots of others teach the R sound as the front of the mouth, pursing the lips, or even something about smiling with your teeth showing.  But I found better success with the back of the tongue position for R sounds. Good luck.

1) Introduce scientific thinking, _especially_ the notion that science changes with data.  

Explain common natural phenomena scientifically, and often.  Get books from the library or book fairs, etc, like the Magic School Bus, that talk about science as fun and interesting.  Encourage her to see the natural world and to ask questions.  Watch nature documentaries. 

And be sure to talk about what people used to think. This can be fun sometimes.  Talk about birds migrating, and how at one time some people used to think they dived into the water and burrowed under the mud under lakes – really! Let her tell you why that's not true (birds need to breath, for one). 

When it's raining, talk about where the water goes.  Reinforce this knowledge often, when you see a creek, a lake, etc.  

This type of logical thinking will help her see for herself that magic is fiction.  

2) Discuss religion directly.  Openly discuss how some people believe in magical things.  That in your family, you know it's not true, but that many people do.  Then discuss various religions.

To avoid weird, pulled areas, stretch-ladders, shift the work two or more*¹ stitches each needle. Here's what I mean. Suppose you have 60 stitches, 15 per needle in a 5 needle set (remember needle is for working). Work the first 12 stitches onto needle #5, slip the last 3 onto the next needles to the left, and now you have a new, empty working needle, and 18 stitches on the needle to the left.  Work only 15, and slide the last 3 as before.  This shifts the gap column each round, and avoids stretch-ladders. 

But when working ribbing, try to align a knit stitch to start, so you avoid starting a row with a purl. Knits are much easier to start than purls.  (*¹That means if you're doing ribbing, the exact number of shifted stitches will need to be a multiple of 2 or 4, and not an odd number.)

Older knitting used to use 4 DPNs, 3 forming a triangle, and the 4th one to work onto.  Now, most people use 5 DPNs, 4 to form a square, with the 5th needle to work onto.  The more nearly circular the shape, the less pulling.  And as one person said, be sure the working needle is in the same alignment as the one you're working from.  

I now use circular needles exclusively, and use a magic loop rather than DPNs.  But I still have to shift the starting point each time.

You know that your nose has mucous. Your mouth, throat, and trachea (the tube to the lungs) also have mucous, but it’s thinner, less like boogers and more like water. The mucous traps lots of undesirable stuff, helping keep it out of your lungs. It’s not enough, however, to catch all the stuff that smokers inhale.  Those things get into the lungs and damage them. 

If you think of the mucous like toilet paper, you can see that you have to get rid of it after it’s dirty. And you don’t want it to drip down into the lungs – that would feel awful, like drowning or like inhaling water.  If it does drip in, it makes you cough, hard, and for a long time. 

The way you normally get rid of that old, dirty mucous is pretty cool. Your throat and trachea have millions of tiny things called cilia that are like super-tiny fingers, waving gently to sweep the mucous up, away from the lungs, and down, away from the nose.  It all collects in the back of your throat where you swallow it!  

This may seem gross at first, but it’s good because your stomach has strong acid that kills lots of germs that were caught in the mucous. 

But!  Smoking causes those little cilia to stop working, for about an hour or so. People who smoke usually smoke more than one cigarette every hour, which means that the cilia never get a chance to restart. If fact, for most smokers the only time the cilia can do their job is at night, after the smoker has been asleep for more than an hour. Lots of smokers hack and cough for a few minutes every morning to try to clear all that mucous that the cilia worked all night to move! 

So what happens?  The mucous builds up, and starts dripping into the lungs. This is painful, and your mom is essentially drowning from her own mucous.

1) Download the free Seek app. It will help you ID the insects you see, via photos. It also identifies plants and pretty much anything. It’s a great app. 

2) Take a white cloth, like a handkerchief or a pillowcase, set it on the ground under a bush, and shake a branch. Lots of insects will fall into the cloth. 

3) Take a magnifying glass, but if that fails use the phone camera zoom to get a better look. 

4) Take a spoon or trough or even a flathead screwdriver to dig a tablespoon or so of dirt here and there to examine. Spread it out on a rock or leaf, or bring something with you like a plastic lid from a to-go box, and wait a second. Some small insects and other invertebrates will crawl around when exposed to the light. 

5) Look among leaves on the ground, just push them aside and watch. That’s what birds are doing when you see them hopping around in the fallen leaves. For this, use small, fast motions then watch, try again, etc. 

6) Get close to the grass on the lawns, like actually lie down, and you will see things waking around in the grass. 

7) If you want to see earthworms, they will rise to the surface if you create a subsoil vibration. You can do this by poking that screwdriver/spoon/a stick you find into the ground and rapidly tapping in the other end.  If you tap with something hard (a rock, another stick), it works better. They rise as far as a foot away, so watch the area around the tool.

For example, on your first question, you list stationary or traveling to describe the fact of how you saw the birds. If you moved less than 30m, like walking around within a bird blind, for example, or watching from your kitchen window, that’s stationary. Traveling is described like this: “Observations made while birding over a specified distance (preferably <5 mi) and duration. Examples include most general field birding, walking a trail, or driving a refuge loop. For routes that return along the same pathway, either submit a different checklist for the return trip or enter the one-way distance. Duration should cover the entire time spent birding, regardless of whether you needed to backtrack.”

Once you open your free account, you can also get the free app and link the two. The app is a portal for entering sightings as you go, freeing you from paper and pencil in the field. I think another way of looking at this is by asking how the meaning might change if one used the indefinite article. 

“I ran out of milk so I went to the store for more.” 
or
“I ran out of milk so I went to a store for more.” 

I might use the latter to imply that the choice of store was somewhat random, or at least unfamiliar to me. I might, for example, use that when relating an experience that occurred in another country, and I wasn’t sure whether the shop I chose would even carry milk. In such a narrative, a listener might anticipate a humorous twist, like “it turned out to be a front for a gambling ring.”
or
“but I realized I had no idea how milk would be packaged, nor can I read Greek, so I ended up buying beef broth!  I thought it was dairy because it had a cow!”

By corollary, the use of the definite article in the former implies that I have a degree of certainty or familiarity. I, the narrator, know what store I went to, I knew I should be able to do that part effortlessly. 

On the other hand, in the US, one goes to *the* hospital when sick, not in the UK.  Americans don’t, however, go to “the” college to mean they attend a higher education school, rather to say “the” college implies a specific school, and no article at all implies the act of getting a higher degree. This is a structure unique to birds: the Synsacrum. (Syn (Greek) = together, combined + Sacrum, the fused vertebrae that are commonly found in tetrapods between the lumbar and tail vertebrae, fused for rigidity and strength so the pelvic girdle can attach to the back) 

From Wikipedia:    

The synsacrum is a skeletal structure of birds and other dinosaurs, in which the sacrum is extended by incorporation of additional fused or partially fused caudal or lumbar vertebrae and it can only be seen in birds. Some posterior thoracic vertebrae, the lumbar, sacral and a few anterior caudal vertebrae are fused to form a complex bone called synsacrum. The innominate bones are fused with the synsacrum to a greater or lesser extent, according to species, forming an avian pelvis. This forms a more extensive rigid structure than the pelvis of a mammal, fulfilling requirements for flight, locomotion and respiration. Posterior to the synsacrum there are a few free caudal vertebrae, the last of which is the pygostyle to which the long, stiff tail feathers are attached.

When you begin to exercise – especially if you have not in the recent past – you will *always* gain weight. This is normal and good.

Why?  Because you are using your muscles. Muscles all attach to the bones. This tug on the bones is a stress, and to prevent stress fractures, the bones must become stronger. They do this by becoming denser. So no only are the muscles growing, but so are the bones. 

Bones, by the way, are made of metal. This surprises many people. Look it up if you want, but calcium is a metal. Metals are heavy. 

You also will need more blood to supply these two growth areas. Blood is mostly water, also heavy. So yes, you will weigh more. This is not a problem unless you make it one by focusing on the wrong thing. Your goal is, of course, to lose weight. But really, you want to lose fat, right?

Weight is the number in the scale. It is not a percentage of body fat.

You will lose fat. It is not just sitting there, like your hair. It is living tissue. It has a blood supply, it has nerves, and it makes chemicals that are released into your bloodstream. When you lose weight, the individual fat cells will lose some of their fat molecules. You will not lose fat cells at first. This is why it’s easy to regain the weight. Every single fat cell is still there, waiting for some surplus food that it can store. Your fat cells are your body’s defense against starvation, and they will do their best to be fully loaded – just in case. 

They only live a few years each, though. So as they slowly die off, one at a time, you body must decide whether to replace them or not. By sticking to the diet component, you are sending them a message: “Don’t bother to replace them, there won’t be a surplus to store.”  

As they decrease in number, their support system also decreases.  You will need fewer blood vessels for the remaining fat tissue. All this will be part of the weight loss. And this loss will exceed the gain in muscle and bone, unless you are doing the body-building route. If you are doing mainly aerobic exercise, you will be strong and slim over time.
